questions.q: A 45-year-old painter cannot initiate abduction of the arm and has pain over the lateral shoulder. Which rotator cuff muscle is most likely torn?
questions.why: The supraspinatus initiates the first roughly 15 degrees of abduction and is the most commonly torn cuff muscle because it is compressed under the acromion. Infraspinatus and teres minor are external rotators, so their loss shows up as weak external rotation, not failed initiation of abduction. Subscapularis is the only internal rotator of the cuff and is tested with the lift-off test.

questions.q: A fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus most directly threatens which nerve?
questions.why: The axillary nerve wraps the surgical neck with the posterior circumflex humeral artery, so injury causes deltoid weakness and numbness over the lateral shoulder 'badge' patch. The radial nerve is at risk at the midshaft spiral groove, not the surgical neck. The median nerve travels medially in the arm and is threatened at the elbow or wrist. The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis and is rarely injured by proximal humeral fracture.

questions.q: Blood moving from the right atrium into the right ventricle passes through which structure?
questions.why: The tricuspid (right atrioventricular) valve separates right atrium from right ventricle. The mitral valve is the left-sided AV valve. The pulmonary valve sits downstream, between right ventricle and pulmonary trunk. The aortic valve guards the left ventricular outflow.

questions.q: A typist reports numbness of the thumb, index, middle, and half the ring finger, with weak thumb opposition. Which structure is compressed?
choices: Radial nerve in the spiral groove
Median nerve in the carpal tunnel
questions.why: The median nerve runs with nine flexor tendons under the flexor retinaculum; compression there gives that exact lateral three-and-a-half digit sensory pattern plus thenar weakness. Ulnar compression at Guyon canal affects the little finger and medial ring finger. Radial injury in the spiral groove causes wrist drop, not thenar loss. A C8 radiculopathy follows a dermatome down the medial forearm, not a carpal tunnel distribution.

questions.q: In which layer of the epidermis does mitosis that renews the skin occur?
questions.why: The stratum basale sits on the basement membrane and holds the dividing keratinocyte stem cells and melanocytes. The stratum spinosum is where cells are already migrating upward and linked by desmosomes. The stratum granulosum is where keratohyalin granules form and nuclei degrade. The stratum corneum is dead, flattened, keratin-filled cells.

questions.q: Growth in the length of a long bone during childhood occurs at the:
questions.why: The epiphyseal (growth) plate is hyaline cartilage that proliferates and is replaced by bone, lengthening the diaphysis until it fuses. The periosteum adds appositional width, not length. The medullary cavity holds marrow. The endosteum lines the marrow cavity and participates in remodeling, not longitudinal growth.

questions.q: McBurney point, the classic surface landmark for appendiceal tenderness, lies in which abdominal region?
questions.why: McBurney point is one-third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, in the right lower quadrant where the appendix arises from the cecum. The left lower quadrant is classic for diverticulitis. The right upper quadrant holds liver and gallbladder. The left upper quadrant holds stomach and spleen.

questions.q: A patient cannot wrinkle the forehead, close the eye, or smile on the right side, but sensation of the face is intact. Which cranial nerve is affected?
questions.why: Cranial nerve VII (facial) supplies the muscles of facial expression; a peripheral lesion spares sensation and involves the forehead. Cranial nerve V carries facial sensation and powers the muscles of mastication. Cranial nerve III moves the eye and raises the lid but does not move the cheek or lips. Cranial nerve XII moves the tongue.

questions.q: Bile leaving the gallbladder travels first through which duct?
questions.why: The cystic duct drains the gallbladder and joins the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct. The common hepatic duct carries bile coming down from the liver, before the gallbladder contribution. The common bile duct is downstream of that junction. The pancreatic duct carries pancreatic enzymes and joins the bile duct at the ampulla of Vater.

questions.q: Within the femoral triangle, moving from lateral to medial, the order of structures is:
questions.why: The mnemonic NAVEL runs lateral to medial: nerve, artery, vein, empty space, lymphatics. That is why a femoral venous stick is placed medial to the palpated pulse. The reversed orders would place the vein or artery lateral to the nerve, which risks arterial puncture when aiming medially.

questions.q: The phrenic nerve, whose loss abolishes spontaneous diaphragmatic breathing, arises from which spinal segments?
questions.why: The phrenic nerve arises from C3, C4, and C5 roots; the saying is 'C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive.' A cord lesion at C1 to C2 also paralyzes the diaphragm, but by cutting the descending drive above those roots rather than by containing their origin. T1 to T4 supply intercostals. C6 to C8 supply upper limb muscles, not the diaphragm.

questions.q: An indirect inguinal hernia passes through the deep inguinal ring alongside which structure in the male?
questions.why: In the male the inguinal canal transmits the spermatic cord, so an indirect hernia follows the cord through the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. The round ligament occupies the canal in the female. The femoral vein passes under the inguinal ligament in the femoral sheath, the route of a femoral hernia. The ureter is retroperitoneal and never enters the inguinal canal.

questions.q: Occlusion of the left anterior descending coronary artery most directly deprives which region of myocardium?
choices: Anterior wall and anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum
Posterior wall of the left ventricle
Lateral wall of the left ventricle
questions.why: The LAD runs in the anterior interventricular groove and feeds the anterior left ventricular wall, the apex, and most of the septum. The SA node and right atrium are supplied by the right coronary artery in most people. The posterior wall is usually right coronary or posterior descending territory. The lateral wall belongs to the left circumflex.

questions.q: A patient has a wide-based unsteady gait, intention tremor, and cannot perform rapid alternating movements. Which structure is damaged?
questions.why: The cerebellum coordinates timing and smoothness of movement and balance, so lesions give ataxia, intention tremor, and dysdiadochokinesia. The occipital lobe handles vision. The medulla houses cardiorespiratory centers and its injury is life-threatening in a different way. The hypothalamus regulates temperature, hunger, and endocrine output, not gait coordination.

questions.q: Broca area, whose damage produces halting nonfluent speech with preserved comprehension, is located in the:
questions.why: Broca area lies in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere and drives speech production. The superior temporal gyrus contains Wernicke area, whose damage gives fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension. The postcentral gyrus is primary somatosensory cortex. Occipital association cortex processes vision.

questions.q: The triangular region of the bladder bounded by the two ureteral orifices and the internal urethral orifice is called the:
questions.why: The trigone is that smooth triangle, clinically important because it is a common site of infection and tumor and does not have rugae. The detrusor is the smooth muscle of the bladder wall. The fundus is the posterior bladder surface. Rugal folds are the collapsible mucosal folds elsewhere in the bladder that let it expand.

questions.q: Deep gluteal pain radiating down the posterior thigh from compression of a nerve as it exits the greater sciatic foramen most likely involves the nerve passing beneath which muscle?
questions.why: The sciatic nerve typically exits inferior to the piriformis, so piriformis hypertrophy or spasm compresses it. Gluteus maximus overlies the region but is superficial to the nerve and not the classic compressor. Obturator internus and quadratus femoris lie deeper and inferior and are not the usual culprits in this syndrome.

questions.q: The anterior cruciate ligament chiefly prevents which motion?
choices: Posterior translation of the tibia on the femur
Anterior translation of the tibia on the femur
questions.why: The ACL runs from the anterior tibia to the posterolateral femur and blocks the tibia sliding forward, which is why the anterior drawer and Lachman tests detect its rupture. Posterior translation is resisted by the PCL. Valgus stress is resisted by the medial collateral ligament and varus stress by the lateral collateral ligament.

questions.q: An aspirated peanut most often lodges in the right mainstem bronchus because it is:
choices: Longer and more horizontal than the left
Wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left
Located below the level of the carina by several centimeters
questions.why: The right mainstem bronchus is wider, shorter, and takes off at a steeper angle, so gravity and airflow favor it. Describing it as longer and more horizontal describes the left bronchus, which arcs over the heart. It is not narrower than the left. Both bronchi begin at the carina, so depth below the carina is not the distinguishing feature.

questions.q: The isthmus of the thyroid gland normally lies anterior to which structure?
choices: The second and third tracheal rings
questions.why: The isthmus crosses the trachea at roughly the second and third rings, which is why it is displaced or divided during a surgical tracheostomy. The cricoid cartilage sits just above it and is the landmark for cricothyrotomy. The thyroid cartilage and hyoid bone are higher in the neck, above the gland entirely.

questions.q: From the skull inward, the meningeal layers are ordered:
choices: Dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater
Pia mater, dura mater, arachnoid mater
Arachnoid mater, dura mater, pia mater
Dura mater, pia mater, arachnoid mater
questions.why: Dura is the tough outer layer against bone, arachnoid is the middle web-like layer, and pia clings directly to brain surface; cerebrospinal fluid occupies the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia. The other sequences misplace pia, which by definition is the innermost layer adherent to neural tissue.

questions.q: A patient struck at the temple has a brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval, then rapid deterioration. A lens-shaped hematoma is seen. Which vessel is torn?
questions.why: An epidural hematoma is arterial bleeding from the middle meningeal artery under the thin pterion, giving a biconvex collection limited by suture lines and a classic lucid interval. Torn bridging veins cause a crescent-shaped subdural hematoma with slower onset. Anterior cerebral artery rupture would bleed into subarachnoid space or parenchyma. The cavernous sinus is a venous channel, not a source of epidural arterial bleeding.

questions.q: The biceps brachii produces which two actions at once?
questions.why: The biceps inserts on the radial tuberosity, so it flexes the elbow and is the strongest supinator, the reason it is used to turn a screwdriver clockwise with the right hand. Extension of the elbow is triceps action. Pronation is pronator teres and pronator quadratus. The biceps does not cross the wrist joint.

questions.q: The hepatic portal vein delivers to the liver blood that has just drained from the:
questions.why: The portal vein is formed by the splenic and superior mesenteric veins and carries nutrient-rich, drug-laden blood from the gut and spleen to the liver for first-pass processing. The lungs drain to the left atrium by pulmonary veins. The kidneys drain into the inferior vena cava. Coronary venous blood returns via the coronary sinus into the right atrium.

questions.q: Which zone of the adrenal gland secretes aldosterone?
questions.why: The outermost zona glomerulosa makes mineralocorticoids, chiefly aldosterone. The zona fasciculata makes glucocorticoids such as cortisol. The zona reticularis makes adrenal androgens. The medulla is modified sympathetic tissue that releases epinephrine and norepinephrine.

questions.q: Which ribs are classified as true ribs?
questions.why: Ribs 1 to 7 attach to the sternum by their own costal cartilage and are called true or vertebrosternal. Ribs 8 to 10 are false ribs sharing the cartilage above them. Ribs 11 and 12 are floating ribs with no anterior attachment. Stopping at rib 5 leaves out two pairs with direct sternal cartilage.

questions.q: The adult vertebral column contains how many cervical, thoracic, and lumbar vertebrae respectively?
questions.why: There are 7 cervical, 12 thoracic (one per rib pair), and 5 lumbar vertebrae, then the fused sacrum and coccyx. The other orders shuffle those counts; the thoracic number is anchored by the 12 rib pairs, and all mammals from giraffes to humans have 7 cervical vertebrae.

questions.q: A patient who fell on an outstretched hand has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. Which bone is most likely fractured?
questions.why: The scaphoid forms the floor of the snuffbox, and its retrograde blood supply makes a missed fracture a risk for avascular necrosis. Lunate injury typically presents as dislocation with median nerve symptoms on the volar side. Hook of hamate fractures hurt in the hypothenar area from racquet or bat handles. Triquetral fractures hurt on the dorsal ulnar wrist, not in the snuffbox.

questions.q: The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon is the common insertion of which muscles?
choices: Tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus
Flexor hallucis longus and tibialis posterior
questions.why: Gastrocnemius and soleus, the triceps surae, share the calcaneal tendon and plantarflex the ankle; rupture gives a positive Thompson test. Tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus dorsiflex and insert on the dorsum of the foot. The peroneals evert and pass behind the lateral malleolus. Flexor hallucis longus and tibialis posterior run behind the medial malleolus to the plantar foot.

questions.q: The sinoatrial node is located in the:
choices: Wall of the right atrium near the opening of the superior vena cava
questions.why: The SA node sits in the upper right atrial wall at the junction with the superior vena cava, which is why right atrial or proximal right coronary problems disturb the rate. The interventricular septum carries the bundle of His and its branches. The left atrial appendage is a thrombus site in atrial fibrillation, not a pacemaker. The right ventricular floor contains Purkinje fibers, a downstream backup pacemaker.

questions.q: The glomerulus and Bowman capsule of the nephron are located in the:
questions.why: All renal corpuscles sit in the cortex; only the loops of Henle and collecting ducts dip into the medulla to build the concentration gradient. The renal pelvis and calyces are urine-collecting spaces lined with transitional epithelium and contain no filtering units.

questions.q: Chyme leaving the stomach passes through which sphincter and into which structure?
choices: Lower esophageal sphincter into the fundus
Sphincter of Oddi into the jejunum
questions.why: The pylorus regulates gastric emptying into the duodenum, the first segment of small intestine. The lower esophageal sphincter is the entrance to the stomach, not the exit. The ileocecal valve is the small-to-large intestine junction far downstream. The sphincter of Oddi controls bile and pancreatic secretions entering the duodenum, not gastric contents.

questions.q: Striking the 'funny bone' at the medial epicondyle produces tingling in the little finger because it compresses the:
questions.why: The ulnar nerve is superficial in the cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle and supplies the little finger and medial half of the ring finger. The median nerve passes anteriorly through the cubital fossa. The radial nerve lies laterally. The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve supplies forearm skin only and would not produce finger symptoms or intrinsic hand weakness.

questions.q: A plane that divides the body into right and left portions is the:
questions.why: The sagittal plane runs front to back dividing right from left; the midsagittal plane makes equal halves. The transverse plane divides superior from inferior. The coronal (frontal) plane divides anterior from posterior. An oblique plane is any angled cut and is not defined by a specific right-left division.

questions.q: Which organ is retroperitoneal?
questions.why: The kidneys lie behind the peritoneum against the posterior body wall, which is why a flank approach reaches them without entering the peritoneal cavity. The stomach, transverse colon, and spleen are intraperitoneal and suspended by mesentery or ligaments.

questions.q: Which rotator cuff muscle, along with infraspinatus, externally rotates the humerus?
questions.why: Teres minor joins infraspinatus as an external rotator and is tested with the arm at the side resisting outward rotation. Supraspinatus abducts. Subscapularis internally rotates. Latissimus dorsi is not part of the cuff at all and extends, adducts, and internally rotates the arm.

questions.q: The circle of Willis connects the two anterior cerebral arteries by way of the:
questions.why: The single anterior communicating artery bridges the left and right anterior cerebral arteries and is a common aneurysm site. The posterior communicating arteries link the internal carotid system to the posterior cerebral arteries. The basilar artery is formed by the two vertebrals and feeds the posterior circulation. The middle cerebral artery is a terminal branch, not a connector.

questions.q: Blunt trauma over the left ninth to eleventh ribs raises concern for injury to which organ?
questions.why: The spleen sits in the left upper quadrant deep to ribs 9 to 11 and is the most commonly injured solid organ in blunt left-sided trauma. The liver occupies the right upper quadrant under the right lower ribs. The pancreas is deep and midline, injured more by direct epigastric compression. The right kidney is on the opposite side.

questions.q: Which auditory ossicle transmits vibration directly to the oval window of the cochlea?
questions.why: The chain runs malleus to incus to stapes, and the stapes footplate rocks in the oval window to start the fluid wave in the cochlea. The malleus is attached to the tympanic membrane. The incus is the middle link. The tympanic membrane is not an ossicle; it is the eardrum that drives the malleus.

questions.q: The region of the retina with the highest visual acuity, packed almost entirely with cones, is the:
questions.why: The fovea within the macula has the densest cone packing and no overlying cell layers, producing sharpest central vision. The optic disc is the blind spot where axons exit and has no photoreceptors. The peripheral retina is rod-dominant, good for dim light and motion. The ora serrata is the anterior serrated edge of the retina.

questions.q: The thoracic duct returns lymph to the venous circulation at the:
choices: Junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins
Superior vena cava at the level of the carina
Junction of the right internal jugular and right subclavian veins
questions.why: The thoracic duct drains roughly three-quarters of the body and empties at the left venous angle. It does not enter the right atrium or the superior vena cava directly. The right venous angle receives the much smaller right lymphatic duct, which drains only the right head, neck, arm, and upper right thorax.

questions.q: The brachial plexus is formed from the ventral rami of which spinal nerves?
questions.why: Roots C5 through T1 form the trunks, divisions, cords, and branches that supply the upper limb. C1 to C4 form the cervical plexus, which includes the phrenic nerve. T1 to T4 are intercostal nerves apart from the T1 contribution. C3 to C7 mixes segments from two different plexuses.

questions.q: The trachea bifurcates at the carina, located at approximately which vertebral level in the adult?
questions.why: The carina lies at the sternal angle, level with the T4 to T5 intervertebral disc, a landmark also used for the aortic arch. C6 is the level where the larynx becomes trachea and where the cricoid ring sits. T1 is at the thoracic inlet, too high. T8 is near the caval hiatus of the diaphragm, well below the bifurcation.

questions.q: A mass in the head of the pancreas commonly causes painless jaundice because it compresses the:
questions.why: The distal common bile duct runs through the head of the pancreas, so a mass there obstructs bile flow and produces jaundice with a palpable distended gallbladder. Portal vein compression causes ascites and varices, not jaundice. The splenic artery runs along the superior body and tail. Obstructing only the pancreatic duct causes pancreatitis and malabsorption, not jaundice.

questions.q: The safe site for a deltoid intramuscular injection is located:
choices: 2 to 3 finger widths below the acromion process, in the lateral midline of the arm
At the insertion of the deltoid on the deltoid tuberosity
questions.why: Injecting about 2 inches (5 cm), roughly 2 to 3 finger widths, below the acromion in the thickest lateral bulk keeps the needle away from the axillary nerve and the bursa. Over the acromion there is bone and no muscle. At the deltoid tuberosity the muscle is thin and the radial nerve is closer. The posterior axillary fold contains vessels and nerves and is never an intramuscular site.

questions.q: The resting membrane potential of a typical neuron is about negative 70 millivolts primarily because:
choices: Sodium ions leak freely into the cell at rest
The membrane is far more permeable to potassium than to sodium at rest
Chloride is actively pumped out of the cell
questions.why: Potassium leak channels dominate resting permeability, so the membrane potential sits near the potassium equilibrium potential of about negative 90 millivolts, pulled slightly positive by small sodium leak. Sodium permeability at rest is low, not high. Chloride distributes largely passively in most neurons. Calcium channels are essentially closed at rest, and calcium is kept very low intracellularly.

questions.q: Each cycle of the sodium-potassium ATPase moves:
questions.why: Three sodium ions leave and two potassium ions enter per ATP hydrolyzed, making the pump electrogenic and contributing a few millivolts of negativity. Reversing the direction would collapse the gradients the cell depends on. A one-for-one exchange would be electroneutral and would not maintain the osmotic and electrical setup the cell needs.

questions.q: The rapid upstroke of a neuronal action potential is produced by:
questions.why: Once threshold near negative 55 millivolts is reached, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium rushes in down both its chemical and electrical gradients. Potassium efflux drives repolarization and the afterhyperpolarization, not the upstroke. Chloride influx is inhibitory and hyperpolarizing. Calcium movement matters at the synaptic terminal and in cardiac muscle, not for the neuronal upstroke.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is released at the skeletal neuromuscular junction?
questions.why: Motor neurons release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors of the motor end plate, which is why neuromuscular blockers and organophosphates act there. Norepinephrine is the main postganglionic sympathetic transmitter to smooth muscle and glands. Glutamate is the principal excitatory transmitter in the central nervous system. Dopamine acts centrally in motor and reward pathways.

questions.q: According to the sliding filament model, muscle shortening occurs because:
choices: Actin and myosin filaments each shorten
Myosin heads pull actin filaments toward the center of the sarcomere
The A band shortens while the I band stays constant
questions.why: Filament lengths do not change; myosin cross-bridges ratchet actin inward so the Z discs approach each other, narrowing the I band and H zone while the A band stays the same width. Saying the A band shortens reverses that observation. Z discs remain intact structures anchoring the thin filaments.

questions.q: In skeletal muscle, calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum initiates contraction by binding to:
questions.why: Calcium binds troponin C, which shifts tropomyosin off the actin binding sites so cross-bridges can form. Myosin heads bind ATP and actin, not calcium. Tropomyosin is moved by troponin rather than binding calcium itself. Calcium does not bind actin directly in skeletal muscle regulation.

questions.q: A patient has a heart rate of 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 mL. What is the cardiac output?
questions.why: Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume: 70 times 70 mL equals 4900 mL/min, or 4.9 L/min, right in the normal 4 to 8 L/min range. The 0.49 answer misplaces the decimal by a factor of ten. The 1.4 answer adds instead of multiplying in effect. The 10 L/min figure would require roughly double this stroke volume or rate.

questions.q: The Frank-Starling relationship states that within physiologic limits, increased venous return leads to:
choices: Increased stroke volume because greater sarcomere stretch improves cross-bridge overlap
Decreased stroke volume because the ventricle is overfilled
Increased heart rate through vagal withdrawal
Decreased afterload on the left ventricle
questions.why: More end-diastolic volume stretches the myocardium toward optimal filament overlap and calcium sensitivity, so contraction is stronger. Overfilling only reduces output past the descending limb, outside normal physiology. Rate changes from venous return are the Bainbridge reflex, a separate phenomenon. Afterload is determined mainly by arterial pressure and vascular resistance, not preload.

questions.q: A sudden fall in blood pressure is detected by baroreceptors located in the carotid sinus and aortic arch. The immediate reflex response is:
choices: Increased parasympathetic output to the heart
Increased sympathetic output causing tachycardia and vasoconstriction
Decreased renin release from the kidney
questions.why: Reduced stretch means reduced baroreceptor firing, which disinhibits the vasomotor center, raising sympathetic tone to speed the heart, increase contractility, and constrict vessels. Increasing vagal tone would slow the heart and worsen the hypotension. Renin release rises, not falls, with low perfusion. Respiratory changes are not the primary baroreflex output.

questions.q: A patient's blood pressure is 120/60 mmHg. What is the approximate mean arterial pressure?
questions.why: Mean arterial pressure is roughly diastolic plus one-third of the pulse pressure: 60 plus one-third of 60, which is 60 plus 20, equals 80 mmHg. Answering 60 uses diastolic alone. Answering 90 uses the simple arithmetic average, which overestimates because diastole occupies more of the cardiac cycle. Answering 70 underweights the pulse pressure contribution.

questions.q: The P wave on an electrocardiogram represents:
questions.why: The P wave is atrial depolarization spreading from the SA node. Ventricular depolarization is the QRS complex, which is larger because of greater ventricular muscle mass. The T wave is ventricular repolarization. Atrial repolarization exists but is buried within the QRS complex and is not separately visible.

questions.q: The plateau phase of the ventricular myocyte action potential, which prolongs contraction and prevents tetany, is produced by:
choices: Calcium influx through L-type channels balancing potassium efflux
Continued sodium influx with no potassium movement
Closure of all ion channels simultaneously
questions.why: Slow L-type calcium current offsets outward potassium current, holding the membrane near zero for roughly 200 milliseconds and producing a long refractory period. Fast sodium channels have already inactivated by then. Chloride contributes only a small early repolarizing notch. If all channels closed, the membrane would simply return to rest, not hold a plateau.

questions.q: Rising temperature, rising carbon dioxide, and falling pH in exercising muscle shift the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve:
choices: Left, increasing hemoglobin affinity for oxygen
Right, decreasing hemoglobin affinity so more oxygen is unloaded
Not at all, since affinity is fixed
questions.why: This is the Bohr effect: acid, heat, carbon dioxide, and 2,3-BPG shift the curve right so hemoglobin gives up oxygen where tissue demand is highest. A leftward shift occurs with alkalosis, hypothermia, and fetal hemoglobin and would hold oxygen tighter, the wrong direction for exercising tissue. Affinity is not fixed, and the curve shifts horizontally, not vertically.

questions.q: A patient hypoventilating after an opioid overdose has an arterial pH of 7.21 and a PaCO2 of 68 mmHg. This represents:
questions.why: Retained carbon dioxide combines with water to form carbonic acid, lowering pH; a low pH with a high PaCO2 defines respiratory acidosis. Metabolic acidosis would show a low bicarbonate with a low or normal PaCO2 from compensatory hyperventilation. Both alkalosis answers require a pH above 7.45.

questions.q: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla drive ventilation primarily in response to:
choices: A fall in arterial oxygen tension
A rise in hydrogen ion concentration in cerebrospinal fluid from diffused carbon dioxide
questions.why: Carbon dioxide crosses the blood-brain barrier, forms carbonic acid in the cerebrospinal fluid, and the resulting hydrogen ions stimulate the central chemoreceptors; this is the minute-to-minute controller of breathing. Low oxygen is sensed by peripheral carotid and aortic bodies and only becomes a strong drive below about 60 mmHg. Potassium is not a ventilatory chemoreceptor stimulus. Stretch receptors mediate the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex.

questions.q: An adult with a tidal volume of 500 mL, an anatomic dead space of 150 mL, and a respiratory rate of 12 breaths per minute has an alveolar ventilation of:
questions.why: Alveolar ventilation equals rate times the difference between tidal volume and dead space: 12 times 350 mL equals 4200 mL/min. The 6.0 L/min figure is total minute ventilation, which ignores dead space. The 1.8 L/min figure is dead space ventilation alone. The 7.8 L/min figure adds rather than subtracts dead space.

questions.q: Pulmonary surfactant, produced by type II alveolar cells, works by:
choices: Increasing alveolar surface tension to keep alveoli open
Reducing surface tension so alveoli resist collapse and compliance improves
Thickening the respiratory membrane to slow diffusion
questions.why: Surfactant disrupts water hydrogen bonding at the air-liquid interface, lowering surface tension, which by the Laplace relationship stabilizes small alveoli and reduces the work of breathing. Increasing surface tension would promote collapse, the problem in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Surfactant does not thicken the membrane or act on capillary tone.

questions.q: Spirometry shows an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.58 with a normal total lung capacity. This pattern indicates:
choices: A neuromuscular weakness pattern with normal airways
questions.why: A ratio below about 0.70 with preserved or increased lung volumes means airflow limitation, as in asthma or COPD. Restrictive disease reduces FVC and total lung capacity while the ratio stays normal or rises. A normal ratio is 0.75 to 0.80 or higher in young adults. Neuromuscular weakness reduces both values proportionately and lowers total lung capacity.

questions.q: Normal glomerular filtration rate in a healthy young adult is approximately:
questions.why: About 125 mL/min, or roughly 180 L/day, is filtered, of which over 99 percent is reabsorbed to yield 1 to 2 L of urine. A rate of 60 mL/min already signals chronic kidney disease stage 3, and 25 mL/min is stage 4. A rate of 300 mL/min exceeds renal plasma flow available for filtration and is physiologically impossible.

questions.q: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure by which combination of actions?
choices: Systemic vasoconstriction plus stimulation of aldosterone release
Inhibition of antidiuretic hormone plus bradycardia
Direct inhibition of renin with increased urine output
questions.why: Angiotensin II is a potent arteriolar constrictor, stimulates adrenal aldosterone secretion, promotes proximal tubule sodium reabsorption, and triggers thirst and ADH release. Vasodilation with sodium loss describes the opposing natriuretic peptides. It stimulates rather than inhibits ADH. It does inhibit further renin release by negative feedback but that raises, not lowers, retained volume.

questions.q: Antidiuretic hormone concentrates the urine by:
choices: Increasing sodium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb
Inserting aquaporin-2 channels into the collecting duct membrane
Blocking aldosterone at the distal tubule
questions.why: ADH acts at V2 receptors to shuttle aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane of principal cells, letting water follow the medullary osmotic gradient. Sodium transport in the thick ascending limb is driven by the NKCC2 cotransporter, the loop diuretic target. Afferent arteriolar tone changes filtration rate, not urine concentration. ADH does not antagonize aldosterone.

questions.q: Aldosterone acting on the principal cells of the collecting duct causes:
questions.why: Aldosterone increases sodium channels and pumps so sodium and water are retained while potassium and hydrogen ions are secreted, which is why hyperaldosteronism causes hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. The reversed answer describes an aldosterone antagonist such as spironolactone. Calcium and phosphate handling is governed by parathyroid hormone and vitamin D.

questions.q: The countercurrent multiplier that builds the hypertonic medullary gradient depends most directly on:
choices: Water reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Active solute transport out of the water-impermeable thick ascending limb
questions.why: The thick ascending limb pumps sodium, potassium, and chloride into the interstitium while remaining impermeable to water, which is what concentrates the medulla; the descending limb then loses water to that gradient. Proximal tubule reabsorption is isotonic and does not create a gradient. SGLT2 recovers glucose, not medullary tonicity. Glomerular filtration supplies the fluid but does not generate the gradient.

questions.q: Insulin lowers blood glucose in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue chiefly by:
choices: Recruiting GLUT4 transporters to the cell membrane
questions.why: Insulin signaling moves GLUT4-containing vesicles to the surface, letting glucose enter insulin-sensitive tissues. It suppresses, not stimulates, gluconeogenesis. It inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase, reducing fat breakdown. It activates glycogen synthase to store glucose; blocking it would do the opposite.

questions.q: During a prolonged fast, glucagon maintains blood glucose first by:
choices: Increasing renal glucose reabsorption above the transport maximum
questions.why: Glucagon first mobilizes liver glycogen, which sustains glucose for roughly 12 to 24 hours, then shifts to gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis. It does not drive glucose into muscle; that is insulin's job, and muscle glycogen cannot release free glucose anyway. Glucagon opposes insulin. Renal reabsorption cannot exceed the transport maximum to create new glucose.

questions.q: In primary hypothyroidism, laboratory testing typically shows:
choices: Low TSH and low free T4
Low TSH and high free T4
High TSH and low free T4
High TSH and high free T4
questions.why: A failing thyroid produces little T4, and the loss of negative feedback lets the pituitary drive TSH up. Low TSH with low T4 points to a pituitary or hypothalamic cause, called central hypothyroidism. Low TSH with high T4 is primary hyperthyroidism. High TSH with high T4 suggests a rare TSH-secreting adenoma or resistance syndrome.

questions.q: Cortisol released during sustained stress produces which set of effects?
choices: Hypoglycemia, increased protein synthesis, enhanced inflammation
Hypoglycemia, bone growth, increased immune activity
Hyperkalemia, decreased blood pressure, increased eosinophils
Hyperglycemia, protein catabolism, and suppression of inflammation
questions.why: Cortisol raises glucose by gluconeogenesis, breaks down peripheral protein and fat for substrate, and dampens the immune and inflammatory response. It does not cause hypoglycemia or boost protein synthesis. It has mild mineralocorticoid effect that tends toward hypokalemia and higher blood pressure, and it lowers rather than raises eosinophil counts.

questions.q: In response to a falling serum calcium, parathyroid hormone acts to:
choices: Increase bone resorption, increase renal calcium reabsorption, and activate vitamin D
Increase renal calcium excretion and inhibit vitamin D
Increase calcitonin release and deposit calcium in bone
questions.why: PTH raises calcium by three routes: osteoclastic bone resorption, distal tubule calcium reabsorption with phosphate wasting, and stimulation of 1-alpha-hydroxylase to make calcitriol, which boosts gut absorption. Increasing calcium excretion or inhibiting vitamin D would drive calcium lower. Calcitonin is the opposing hormone from thyroid C cells.

questions.q: Gastric parietal cells secrete which two products?
questions.why: Parietal cells use the H+/K+ ATPase to secrete acid and also make intrinsic factor, so their autoimmune destruction produces both achlorhydria and vitamin B12 deficiency. Chief cells make pepsinogen and surface mucous cells make mucus. Gastrin comes from G cells and somatostatin from D cells. Bicarbonate comes mainly from the pancreas and gastric surface mucus layer.

questions.q: Fat entering the duodenum triggers release of which hormone, causing gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion?
questions.why: Cholecystokinin from duodenal I cells contracts the gallbladder, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, and stimulates enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion. Gastrin stimulates gastric acid and is triggered by peptides and stomach distension. Secretin responds to acid and drives bicarbonate-rich pancreatic fluid. Motilin governs the interdigestive migrating motor complex between meals.

questions.q: Bile salts aid fat digestion by:
choices: Chemically cleaving triglycerides into fatty acids
Neutralizing gastric acid in the duodenum
Transporting fatty acids across the enterocyte membrane by active transport
Emulsifying fat into small droplets that increase the surface area for lipase
questions.why: Bile salts are amphipathic detergents; they break large fat globules into micelles so pancreatic lipase has far more surface to work on. They are not enzymes and cleave nothing themselves. Acid neutralization in the duodenum is done by pancreatic and biliary bicarbonate. Fatty acid entry into enterocytes is largely passive diffusion from micelles.

questions.q: Stimulation of beta-1 adrenergic receptors on the heart produces:
questions.why: Beta-1 receptors dominate in the myocardium and increase rate, contractility, and conduction velocity, and also stimulate renin release from the kidney. Bronchodilation is a beta-2 effect in airway smooth muscle. Peripheral vasoconstriction is alpha-1 mediated. Renin release increases rather than decreases with beta-1 stimulation.

questions.q: Parasympathetic slowing of the heart is mediated by which nerve and receptor?
choices: Phrenic nerve acting on nicotinic receptors
Vagus nerve acting on muscarinic receptors
Sympathetic chain acting on alpha-2 receptors
Glossopharyngeal nerve acting on beta-2 receptors
questions.why: The vagus releases acetylcholine onto M2 muscarinic receptors in the SA and AV nodes, slowing rate and conduction, which is why atropine speeds the heart. The phrenic nerve drives the diaphragm and uses nicotinic receptors at muscle. Alpha-2 receptors are presynaptic sympathetic autoreceptors. The glossopharyngeal nerve carries baroreceptor and chemoreceptor afferents, not cardiac motor output.

questions.q: The patellar tendon reflex is a monosynaptic reflex whose sensory receptor is the:
questions.why: Tapping the tendon stretches the quadriceps, the muscle spindle fires through a Ia afferent that synapses directly on the alpha motor neuron, and the muscle contracts. The Golgi tendon organ senses tension and produces an inhibitory, polysynaptic response. Pacinian corpuscles detect vibration and deep pressure. Free nerve endings carry pain and temperature.

questions.q: Myelination speeds nerve conduction because:
choices: It increases the diameter of the axon's cytoplasm
It adds more voltage-gated sodium channels along the entire axon
It allows continuous slow propagation with less energy
It insulates internodal segments so current jumps between nodes of Ranvier
questions.why: Saltatory conduction concentrates voltage-gated sodium channels at the nodes, and the insulated internodes let current flow passively and rapidly between them, reaching up to 120 m/s. Myelin does not change axoplasmic diameter directly. Channels are clustered at nodes rather than spread along the whole axon. Continuous propagation is what unmyelinated fibers do, and it is slower.

questions.q: Chronic hypoxia stimulates increased red blood cell production through release of erythropoietin from the:
choices: Peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney
questions.why: Renal peritubular fibroblast-like cells sense tissue oxygen and release erythropoietin, which is why chronic kidney disease causes anemia. Bone marrow is the target of erythropoietin, not its source. The fetal liver makes it and the adult liver contributes only a small fraction. The anterior pituitary makes trophic hormones such as ACTH and TSH, not erythropoietin.

questions.q: In hemostasis, the final common step of the coagulation cascade is:
choices: Platelet adhesion to exposed collagen by von Willebrand factor
Activation of factor XII by contact with a foreign surface
questions.why: Both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge on factor X, which with factor V generates thrombin, and thrombin polymerizes fibrinogen into a cross-linked fibrin mesh. Platelet adhesion is primary hemostasis, which precedes the cascade. Factor XII contact activation begins the intrinsic pathway, not the common final step. Plasmin dissolves clots during fibrinolysis, the opposite process.

questions.q: A patient with liver failure and a serum albumin of 1.8 g/dL develops peripheral edema because:
choices: Capillary hydrostatic pressure has risen sharply
Plasma oncotic pressure has fallen, so less fluid is drawn back into the capillary
questions.why: Albumin generates most plasma colloid osmotic pressure; when it drops, Starling forces favor net filtration into the interstitium. Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure causes edema in heart failure or venous obstruction, a different mechanism. Lymphatic obstruction causes lymphedema, as in filariasis or after node dissection. Lower interstitial hydrostatic pressure would actually accept more fluid but is not the primary driver here.

questions.q: The body's thermoregulatory set point is controlled by the:
questions.why: The preoptic area of the hypothalamus compares core temperature to a set point and drives sweating, shivering, and cutaneous vasomotor changes; pyrogens raise that set point in fever. The medulla governs cardiorespiratory reflexes. The thalamus relays sensory information including temperature but does not set the target. The pineal gland secretes melatonin for circadian timing.

questions.q: Type I (slow oxidative) skeletal muscle fibers are characterized by:
choices: High mitochondrial density, high myoglobin, and fatigue resistance
Low capillary density and rapid fatigue
Reliance on anaerobic glycolysis for most ATP
The largest fiber diameter and highest force per fiber
questions.why: Type I fibers are built for endurance: many mitochondria, plenty of myoglobin and capillaries, and sustained aerobic ATP production, as in postural muscles. Low capillary density and fast fatigue describe type IIx fibers. Heavy reliance on anaerobic glycolysis is also a fast-twitch trait. Large diameter and peak force belong to fast glycolytic fibers.

questions.q: Most oxygen carried in arterial blood is transported:
choices: Bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells
questions.why: About 98 percent of oxygen is bound to hemoglobin, with each gram carrying roughly 1.34 mL of oxygen; only about 0.3 mL per 100 mL is dissolved in plasma. Bicarbonate is the main transport form of carbon dioxide, not oxygen. Albumin transports drugs, calcium, and bilirubin but does not carry oxygen.

questions.q: According to Poiseuille's relationship, halving the radius of a vessel changes its resistance to flow by a factor of:
questions.why: Resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of radius, so halving radius multiplies resistance by 2 to the fourth power, or 16. A factor of 2 would apply if resistance varied simply with radius. A factor of 4 would apply to a squared relationship, and 8 to a cubed one; neither matches the fourth-power law.

questions.q: A patient has an end-diastolic volume of 120 mL and an end-systolic volume of 50 mL. The ejection fraction is approximately:
questions.why: Stroke volume is 120 minus 50, or 70 mL; ejection fraction is 70 divided by 120, about 58 percent, within the normal 55 to 70 percent range. The 70 percent answer mistakes the stroke volume in mL for the percentage. The 42 percent answer divides end-systolic by end-diastolic volume. The 40 percent answer would indicate systolic heart failure, which these numbers do not show.

questions.q: Ovulation is triggered by:
choices: A fall in estrogen to its lowest level
A surge in progesterone from the corpus luteum
Peak follicle-stimulating hormone on day 1 of the cycle
questions.why: Rising estrogen from the dominant follicle switches to positive feedback and triggers the mid-cycle LH surge, and ovulation follows roughly 24 to 36 hours later. Estrogen is at a peak, not a nadir, just before ovulation. Progesterone rises after ovulation once the corpus luteum forms. FSH rises early in the follicular phase to recruit follicles but does not trigger release.

questions.q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis breathes deeply and rapidly. This Kussmaul respiration represents:
choices: Metabolic compensation for a respiratory acidosis
Respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis
questions.why: Ketoacids lower pH, and blowing off carbon dioxide reduces carbonic acid to pull pH back toward normal; the lungs respond within minutes. Metabolic compensation for respiratory problems is renal and takes days, and the kidneys do not control breathing pattern. Anxiety hyperventilation would produce alkalosis with a normal anion gap. A failing respiratory center would cause hypoventilation, not deep rapid breathing.

questions.q: In the fluid mosaic model, the basic structural framework of the plasma membrane is provided by:
choices: A phospholipid bilayer with hydrophilic heads outward and hydrophobic tails inward
questions.why: Amphipathic phospholipids self-assemble into a bilayer that forms the permeability barrier. Cholesterol is inserted among the phospholipids to modulate fluidity but does not form the framework. Proteins float within or span the bilayer and handle transport and signaling. The glycocalyx is an outer sugar coat used for recognition and adhesion.

questions.q: The electron transport chain and ATP synthase of a eukaryotic cell are located in the:
questions.why: The cristae of the inner membrane hold the four respiratory complexes and ATP synthase, and the intermembrane space stores the proton gradient. The outer membrane is freely permeable to small molecules through porins. The matrix holds the Krebs cycle enzymes and mitochondrial DNA. The cytosol is where glycolysis occurs.

questions.q: A cell specialized for secreting large amounts of protein hormone would be expected to contain abundant:
questions.why: Ribosomes studding the rough ER synthesize proteins destined for secretion, membranes, or lysosomes. Smooth ER handles lipid and steroid synthesis, calcium storage, and detoxification, and dominates in steroid-producing cells instead. Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and hydrogen peroxide. Centrioles organize the mitotic spindle.

questions.q: The Golgi apparatus functions primarily to:
choices: Modify, sort, and package proteins into vesicles for delivery
Digest worn-out organelles using acid hydrolases
questions.why: The Golgi receives vesicles at the cis face, glycosylates and edits their contents, then buds them from the trans face toward their destination. ATP production is mitochondrial. Transcription happens in the nucleus. Digestion of worn organelles is the job of lysosomes, although the Golgi does produce them.

questions.q: Lysosomes carry out intracellular digestion using enzymes that work best at:
choices: Acidic pH near 5, maintained by a proton pump
Any pH, since they are pH independent
questions.why: A V-type ATPase pumps protons in to hold the lumen near pH 5, the optimum for acid hydrolases, which also limits damage if they leak into the neutral cytosol. Alkaline or neutral optima would leave the enzymes inactive inside the lysosome. Enzyme activity is strongly pH dependent because pH alters ionization and folding.

questions.q: Which feature is present in eukaryotic cells but absent in prokaryotic cells?
questions.why: Prokaryotes keep their circular DNA in a nucleoid with no surrounding membrane and lack all membrane-bound organelles. Both cell types have ribosomes, though prokaryotic ones are 70S versus the eukaryotic 80S, a difference many antibiotics exploit. Both have a plasma membrane and both store genetic information in DNA.

questions.q: A red blood cell placed in a hypertonic salt solution will:
choices: Actively pump sodium inward to equalize
questions.why: Water moves toward the higher solute concentration, so it leaves the cell and the cell crenates. Swelling and hemolysis occur in a hypotonic solution such as pure water. No net change happens only in an isotonic solution such as 0.9 percent saline. Osmosis is passive; the cell does not pump sodium in to fix tonicity.

questions.q: Which statement distinguishes facilitated diffusion from active transport?
choices: Facilitated diffusion requires no membrane protein
Facilitated diffusion moves solute down its concentration gradient without ATP
Facilitated diffusion can concentrate solute against a gradient
Active transport is always faster than facilitated diffusion
questions.why: Both use proteins, but facilitated diffusion is passive and can only move solute downhill, while active transport spends energy to move solute uphill. Saying it needs no protein describes simple diffusion. Concentrating against a gradient is the defining feature of active transport. Speed is not the distinguishing criterion; facilitated diffusion can be very fast.

questions.q: Enzymes increase the rate of a chemical reaction by:
choices: Increasing the free energy released by the reaction
Raising the temperature of the solution
Lowering the activation energy required to reach the transition state
Changing the equilibrium position toward products
questions.why: By stabilizing the transition state, an enzyme reduces the energy barrier so more collisions succeed at body temperature. Enzymes do not change the overall free energy change of a reaction, nor the equilibrium constant; they only shorten the time needed to reach equilibrium. They do not generate heat to speed reactions.

questions.q: A competitive inhibitor added to an enzyme reaction produces which effect on kinetics?
choices: Unchanged Vmax with increased apparent Km
questions.why: A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and is outcompeted by excess substrate, so maximum velocity is still reachable but more substrate is needed, raising apparent Km. Lowered Vmax with unchanged Km is the noncompetitive pattern. Lowered Vmax with lowered Km describes uncompetitive inhibition. No inhibitor raises Vmax.

questions.q: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and yields a net gain per glucose of:
questions.why: Four ATP are produced and two are invested, so the net is 2 ATP, plus 2 NADH and 2 three-carbon pyruvates. FADH2 is generated in the Krebs cycle and in fatty acid oxidation, not in glycolysis. Lactate forms only if fermentation follows under anaerobic conditions. The 36 ATP figure is the total for complete aerobic oxidation of glucose, not for glycolysis alone.

questions.q: One turn of the citric acid cycle, occurring in the mitochondrial matrix, produces:
choices: 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP, and 2 carbon dioxide
6 NADH and 2 FADH2 per glucose molecule entering glycolysis
questions.why: Each acetyl-CoA turn yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP or ATP, and releases 2 carbon dioxide; per glucose the cycle turns twice. The first option undercounts reduced carriers. Pyruvate is a product of glycolysis, not of the cycle. The last option gives per-glucose totals for the cycle but is off and is not a single turn.

questions.q: The final electron acceptor of the mitochondrial electron transport chain is:
questions.why: Oxygen accepts electrons at complex IV and combines with protons to form water; without it the chain backs up and ATP production collapses. NAD+ is a carrier that is regenerated, not a final acceptor. Pyruvate serves as an electron acceptor only in lactate fermentation. Cytochrome c is a mobile intermediate between complexes III and IV.

questions.q: Complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule yields approximately how much ATP by current estimates?
questions.why: Modern accounting gives about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2, minus transport costs, for roughly 30 to 32 ATP. Two ATP is the anaerobic glycolytic yield only. Eight ATP is too low even for glycolysis plus pyruvate oxidation. The 60 to 64 range roughly doubles the true value and matches no standard calculation.

questions.q: The main purpose of lactic acid fermentation in an oxygen-starved muscle cell is to:
choices: Regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can continue producing ATP
Produce large amounts of ATP directly from lactate
Remove carbon dioxide from the cell
questions.why: Without oxygen, NADH cannot be reoxidized by the electron transport chain, so reducing pyruvate to lactate recycles NAD+ and keeps the modest 2 ATP per glucose of glycolysis flowing. Fermentation itself makes no ATP. It produces no carbon dioxide in the lactate pathway. Making glucose from pyruvate is gluconeogenesis, which consumes energy and occurs mainly in the liver.

questions.q: In photosynthesis, the light-dependent reactions in the thylakoid membrane produce:
choices: Only ATP, with no reducing power
questions.why: Splitting water supplies electrons and releases oxygen, while photophosphorylation makes ATP and reduces NADP+ to NADPH. Glucose is made later in the Calvin cycle in the stroma, using that ATP and NADPH. Carbon dioxide and water are inputs, not products. NADPH production is central to the light reactions, so ruling out reducing power is wrong.

questions.q: In double-stranded DNA, the two strands are:
choices: Parallel, with adenine pairing to guanine
Antiparallel, with adenine pairing to uracil
Antiparallel, with adenine pairing to thymine by two hydrogen bonds
Parallel, with cytosine pairing to thymine
questions.why: One strand runs 5-prime to 3-prime while its partner runs the opposite direction, and A pairs with T through two hydrogen bonds while G pairs with C through three, which is why GC-rich DNA has a higher melting temperature. Adenine never pairs with guanine, since two purines are too wide for the helix. Uracil replaces thymine in RNA, not DNA. Cytosine does not pair with thymine.

questions.q: DNA replication is described as semiconservative because each daughter molecule contains:
choices: A patchwork of old and new segments within each strand
One original strand and one newly synthesized strand
questions.why: The Meselson and Stahl experiment confirmed that each helix keeps one parental template and one new strand. Two wholly new strands would be conservative replication. Two original strands would mean no synthesis at all. A patchwork within a single strand describes the dispersive model, which the density data ruled out.

questions.q: During transcription, RNA polymerase:
choices: Synthesizes messenger RNA from a DNA template in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction
Joins amino acids into a polypeptide
Requires a primer laid down by primase
questions.why: RNA polymerase reads the template strand 3-prime to 5-prime and builds mRNA 5-prime to 3-prime, and unlike DNA polymerase it needs no primer. Joining amino acids is translation, done by the ribosome. Copying RNA into DNA is reverse transcription, used by retroviruses and by telomerase in a limited way.

questions.q: During translation, the correct amino acid is brought to the ribosome because:
choices: Messenger RNA binds amino acids directly
The transfer RNA anticodon base-pairs with the messenger RNA codon
Ribosomal RNA reads the amino acid sequence from DNA
The Golgi apparatus matches amino acids to codons
questions.why: Each charged tRNA carries an anticodon complementary to a specific mRNA codon, so base pairing at the A site enforces the genetic code. mRNA carries the message but never binds amino acids itself. rRNA forms the ribosome's structure and catalyzes peptide bonds but does not read DNA. The Golgi acts after translation, on finished proteins.

questions.q: The genetic code is described as degenerate (redundant) because:
choices: One codon can specify several different amino acids
Codons overlap so a base can be read twice
Most amino acids are specified by more than one codon
Some codons specify no amino acid at all
questions.why: With 64 codons for 20 amino acids, most amino acids have two to six synonymous codons, usually differing at the third base, which buffers some point mutations. A single codon never specifies more than one amino acid; the code is unambiguous. The code is nonoverlapping and read in fixed triplets. Stop codons do specify no amino acid, but that is termination, not degeneracy.

questions.q: Deleting a single nucleotide from the middle of a protein-coding sequence most likely produces:
choices: A silent mutation with no change in the protein
A conservative substitution of one similar amino acid
A change only in the last amino acid of the protein
A frameshift that alters every downstream codon
questions.why: Because codons are read in nonoverlapping triplets, inserting or deleting one or two bases shifts the reading frame and garbles everything downstream, often creating a premature stop. Silent mutations come from third-base substitutions that keep the same amino acid. A conservative substitution results from a missense point change. Only a change near the 3-prime end would affect just the last residue.

questions.q: Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles during which phase of mitosis?
questions.why: Anaphase begins when the cohesin holding sister chromatids is cleaved and spindle microtubules pull them apart. Prophase is chromosome condensation and nuclear envelope breakdown. Metaphase is alignment at the equatorial plate. Telophase is the reformation of nuclear envelopes around the two separated sets.

questions.q: Crossing over, which shuffles alleles between homologous chromosomes, occurs during:
questions.why: Homologs synapse as tetrads in prophase I and exchange segments at chiasmata, a major source of genetic variation along with independent assortment. Meiosis II resembles mitosis and separates sister chromatids, with no pairing of homologs. Interphase is when DNA replicates, before homologs pair.

questions.q: Trisomy 21 arises most often from:
choices: A frameshift mutation in chromosome 21 genes
Uniparental disomy from a point mutation
Nondisjunction during meiosis, usually in the maternal oocyte
Crossing over between chromosomes 21 and 14 in every case
questions.why: Failure of chromosome 21 to separate in meiosis leaves a gamete with two copies, and maternal meiosis I nondisjunction accounts for the large majority; risk rises with maternal age. A frameshift changes a single gene, not chromosome number. A translocation involving chromosome 14 explains only a small minority of cases, not every case. Point mutations do not create an extra chromosome.

questions.q: Crossing two heterozygotes for a simple dominant trait (Aa by Aa) gives what phenotypic ratio in the offspring?
questions.why: The genotype ratio is 1 AA to 2 Aa to 1 aa, and because A is dominant, three of four show the dominant phenotype. A 1:1 ratio comes from a test cross of Aa by aa. The 9:3:3:1 ratio is the dihybrid result. The 1:2:1 ratio is the genotype ratio here, or the phenotype ratio when inheritance is incompletely dominant.

questions.q: Two parents heterozygous for cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive condition, are expecting a child. What is the probability the child is an unaffected carrier?
questions.why: The Punnett square gives 1 homozygous normal, 2 heterozygous carriers, and 1 affected, so the chance of being a carrier is 2 in 4, or 1/2. The 1/4 figure is the chance of being affected or of being homozygous normal. The 3/4 figure is the chance of being unaffected by any means. The 2/3 figure applies only after already knowing the child is unaffected.

questions.q: A woman who carries an X-linked recessive allele has children with an unaffected man. What is expected?
choices: All daughters affected, all sons unaffected
Half of sons affected, daughters unaffected but half are carriers
questions.why: Sons get their single X from mother, so half inherit the allele and are affected since they have no second X to mask it. Daughters receive a normal X from father, so none are affected but half are carriers. Daughters cannot all be affected here because the father contributes a normal allele. Affected daughters require an affected father and a carrier mother.

questions.q: A person with blood type AB expresses both A and B antigens on their red cells. This is an example of:
questions.why: Both alleles are fully and simultaneously expressed, which is codominance. Incomplete dominance would blend the two into an intermediate phenotype, as in pink flowers from red and white. Epistasis is one gene masking another gene's expression, such as the Bombay phenotype. Polygenic inheritance involves many genes producing a continuous trait such as height.

questions.q: In a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the recessive phenotype occurs in 1 of every 100 individuals. What is the frequency of heterozygous carriers?
questions.why: If q squared is 0.01 then q is 0.1 and p is 0.9, so 2pq equals 2 times 0.9 times 0.1, or 0.18. The value 0.01 is q squared, the affected frequency. The value 0.10 is q itself, the allele frequency. The value 0.81 is p squared, the homozygous dominant frequency.

questions.q: Repeated antibiotic exposure leaves a bacterial population dominated by resistant organisms. The best explanation is that:
choices: Pre-existing resistant variants survived and reproduced while susceptible ones died
The antibiotic caused the bacteria to develop resistance in response to the threat
Individual bacteria adapted during their lifetime and passed on the acquired trait
Resistance arose because the bacteria needed it
questions.why: Natural selection acts on variation that already exists from random mutation or horizontal gene transfer; the drug only sets which variants reproduce. Antibiotics do not instruct bacteria to become resistant. The idea of adapting during a lifetime and passing that on is Lamarckian and inconsistent with how heredity works. Need does not cause mutation; selection acts after variation appears.

questions.q: The human arm, whale flipper, and bat wing share the same underlying bone arrangement despite different functions. These are:
choices: Analogous structures resulting from convergent evolution
Homologous structures reflecting descent from a common ancestor
Vestigial structures with no current function
questions.why: Shared structure with divergent function indicates common ancestry, the definition of homology. Analogous structures share function but not ancestry, such as insect and bird wings. Vestigial structures are reduced remnants such as the human coccyx. Genetic drift is a random change in allele frequency, unrelated to anatomical comparison.

questions.q: A river permanently divides one squirrel population into two, which diverge over many generations until they can no longer interbreed. This is:
questions.why: Allopatric speciation requires geographic isolation that blocks gene flow while mutation, drift, and selection push the groups apart. Sympatric speciation occurs without physical separation, often by polyploidy or niche differentiation. Artificial selection is human-directed breeding. Directional selection shifts a trait mean but by itself does not create reproductive isolation.

questions.q: In the standard taxonomic hierarchy, which sequence runs from broadest to most specific?
choices: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
questions.why: The full sequence widest to narrowest is domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. The first option runs the wrong direction. The second skips ranks and also runs narrow to broad. The third places order before class, reversing those two ranks.

questions.q: Roughly what proportion of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next level in a food chain?
questions.why: Most energy at each level is lost as heat through metabolism or is never consumed, so about 10 percent is passed upward, which is why food chains rarely exceed four or five levels. Fifty or ninety percent would allow far longer chains and enormous top-predator biomass. Complete transfer would violate the second law of thermodynamics.

questions.q: Gut bacteria that synthesize vitamin K while receiving nutrients from the host illustrate:
questions.why: Both partners benefit, which defines mutualism. Parasitism benefits one at the other's expense, as with tapeworms. Commensalism benefits one while the other is unaffected, such as many skin flora. Competition harms both parties as they contend for the same limited resource.

questions.q: In the nitrogen cycle, nitrogen fixation refers to:
choices: Conversion of ammonia to nitrite and then nitrate by soil bacteria
Conversion of nitrate back to nitrogen gas
Conversion of atmospheric nitrogen gas into ammonia
Release of ammonia from decomposing organic matter
questions.why: Fixation is the reduction of inert N2 to ammonia by bacteria such as Rhizobium or by lightning, making nitrogen biologically usable. Converting ammonia to nitrite and nitrate is nitrification. Returning nitrate to N2 gas is denitrification. Releasing ammonia from dead tissue is ammonification.

questions.q: A population growing logistically levels off as it approaches carrying capacity because:
choices: Mutation rates fall as density increases
The intrinsic rate of increase becomes negative at all densities
Reproduction stops entirely once carrying capacity is reached
Density-dependent factors such as limited food, space, and disease slow growth
questions.why: As density rises, competition, predation, waste, and disease increasingly limit per capita growth until births roughly equal deaths. Mutation rate is unrelated to population density in this model. The intrinsic rate of increase is a constant parameter; it is realized growth that declines. Reproduction continues at carrying capacity, but it is offset by mortality.

questions.q: The three-dimensional folding of a single polypeptide chain, stabilized by disulfide bridges and hydrophobic interactions, is that protein's:
questions.why: Tertiary structure is the overall shape of one chain, held by disulfide bonds, hydrophobic packing, hydrogen bonds, and ionic bridges. Primary structure is simply the amino acid sequence. Secondary structure refers to local alpha helices and beta sheets formed by backbone hydrogen bonds. Quaternary structure requires two or more separate chains assembling, as in hemoglobin.

questions.q: The p53 protein halts the cell cycle at the G1 checkpoint when DNA damage is detected. Loss of functional p53 in a cell most directly results in:
choices: Failure of cytokinesis and multinucleated cells
Division of cells carrying unrepaired DNA damage
Inability to enter S phase at all
Loss of the ability to synthesize ribosomes
questions.why: p53 is the guardian of the genome; without it, damaged cells pass the G1 checkpoint, accumulate mutations, and escape apoptosis, which is why p53 is mutated in roughly half of human cancers. Cytokinesis failure involves the contractile ring and actin-myosin machinery, not p53. Cells lacking p53 enter S phase more readily, not less. Ribosome synthesis is a nucleolar function independent of checkpoint control.
